Big deal.

Thursday was a special day and the climax of the three day event to mark the signing of the UK-Viet Nam Comprehensive Strategic Partnership here in London.

Alongside speaking at the Business Conference attended by hundreds of UK and Vietnamese businesses, I witnessed the Rolls-Royce/Airbus–VietJet contract signing as HM Trade Envoy to Viet Nam.

The contract with VietJet airlines is for the supply of 40 Rolls Royce Trent 7000 engines (to power 20 Airbus A330 neo aircraft) and for 100 Airbus A321neo jets (the latter worth a reported $25bn).

The deal is worth £3.8bn to the Derby based manufacturer, a company I visited a year ago to see for myself the brilliance of their engineering that makes them the global leader that they are.

The deal will benefit not just RR and Airbus (with plants in N Wales and Bristol) but many others too. As with the UK automotive sector, Rolls Royce aero engines has a complex supply chain and I’m proud that includes supplier businesses in Warwick and Leamington (you know who you are).

Such deals take a huge amount of effort to get them over the line. Massive congratulations to Rolls Royce and Airbus. I was proud to represent the UK and join them at the signing ceremony.

I’ll always back British business whether it’s Rolls-Royce and Airbus, Aston Martin and Jaguar Land Rover, or family-run businesses here in Warwick and Leamington. 

There is no silver bullet for transforming the economy. But this is a great achievement and shows what we can accomplish when we work constructively and in good faith with international partners.

It was brilliant to pop down to meet new CEO Anthea and the rest of the team at Eva’s House, a Women’s Aid and Rape Support Centre. We talked about how we can work together to support the domestic violence services here in Redcar and Cleveland. The work they do at Eva’s is vital in our community, from providing refuge and counselling services, to helping women back out into the community through their supported housing scheme, to working with children traumatised by the violence they have experienced.

For far too long, violence against women and girls has been treated as just a sad but inevitable part of society, instead of the national emergency it is. I know so many of us are concerned by the rise in misogyny and violence against women we are seeing normalised on the internet, in our communities and, shockingly, even in schools. We must take a stand now to stamp out violence once and for all. 

That’s why services like Eva’s are key in providing safe spaces for women, and also in encouraging preventative action through the work they do with schools and children as young as primary age to teach them about healthy relationships. 

We spoke about Labour’s mission to halve violence against women and girls in a decade, which is underpinned by the new VAWG strategy we’ll see released later this year and will be a welcome step towards achieving this goal.

But work has already begun, with our plan to introduce domestic abuse specialists into 999 control rooms already being rolled out. We have also pledged £2.2 million to fund the first stages of Raneem’s Law, a law that aims to improve police handling of domestic abuse cases after the tragic murder of Raneem Oudeh and her mother at the hands of Raneem’s ex-husband. 

Our new amendments to the Online Safety Act will also be key in tackling the unregulated violence against women and graphic content we see all across the internet by introducing greater restrictions on illegal content and ensuring children cannot access it.

I had the honour of attending the Service of Thanksgiving for the UDR, and all those who served and gave their lives to defend NI from the scourge of terrorism over the 23 years of the life of the regiment.

Since I became MP for East Antrim, it has been my honour to attend this service held in St Saviours Church in Connor each year.

The most poignant part of the service is when they read out the names of those who were murdered because they dared to serve in the UDR.

Last night I met the widow of one such soldier who was murdered at his own home, leaving his wife and three children. UDR soldiers were targets for terrorists 24 hours a day, not just when they were on patrol.

Over the lifetime of the regiment 40,000 men and women served in the UDR; 198 were murdered during their service but even after they had retired they were still targets. A further 62 were murdered even though they were no longer members.

Hundreds were left maimed as a result of injuries sustained because of terrorist murder attempts. 

It is important we remember the sacrifices made, and it was great to see so many veterans at the service proudly wearing their medals and remembering their fallen comrades.

As The Troubles fade from memory, it is sad to see that there is a generation growing up who don’t even know what the letters UDR stand for let alone the important work they did in securing peace in NI.

I thank Rev Ian Magowan and the local UDR ex members for their commitment to keeping alive this the memory of those who served our country so well in dark times.

We must never forget.

Yesterday afternoon, a small group gathered in Ashington for their second protest in a month.
The good people of our town have endured enormous challenges over the past century, and many continue to live with the legacy of deindustrialisation and poverty. Frustration with successive governments failing to tackle inequality and crumbling public services is understandable and justified.

But let’s be clear: this protest was never about tackling inequality or fighting for better public services. It was led by a banner that was then displayed in the memorial garden bearing the name of a group identified by Hope not Hate as a neo-Nazi organisation.

Whether or not the organisers understood what this group represents, it is completely unacceptable to have such a banner leading a protest in front of a war memorial, let alone for people to pose for photographs with it. The memorial honours more than 1,000 Ashington residents who gave their lives during the two world wars. Their sacrifice was made in the fight against fascism. To use that sacred space to promote an organisation dedicated to spreading it is nothing short of a desecration.

It is also deeply concerning to see so many young children in attendance, exposed to such hateful imagery and rhetoric. The good people of Ashington deserve better than to have their community and their memorial dragged into association with extremism.

The organisers of this protest should apologise without hesitation for this disgraceful act of disrespect.

David Railton KC unveiling the plaque commissioned by the Margate Civic Society in memory of his grandfather The Reverend David Railton MC. 

The Reverend Railton was awarded the Military Cross for acts of outstanding bravery while serving as a padre in the trenches during the First World War. He served as the vicar of the church of Saint John the Baptist, the parish church of Margate between 1920 and 1925 and it was during this time that he successfully campaigned for the creation of the tomb of the Unknown Warrior in Westminster Abbey. 

The Union Flag that Rev. Railton used to cover makeshift altars in the trenches and subsequently adorned the pulpit while he was preaching at St. John’s now hangs, as the ‘Padre’s Flag’, close to the warrior’s grave in the Abbey.

Before enjoying their Christmas dinner, Labour MPs should think long and hard about where that food actually comes from.

It didn't magically appear in Waitrose, or whatever vegan market they shop in - it was grown by British farmers, on British farms.

Those same farming families will soon be forced to sell their farm as a direct result of the changes being brought in by Labour. Who buys it up? Big multinationals, who care nothing for the land or our food security.

Farmers love their farms, and care for the land in a way nobody else could. I love my farm, it's my passion. If farmers go, the countryside we all love goes with them.

I still see people in the media, even MPs, failing to understand. Either they're doing so deliberately, or they're just thick.

The farm is only worth something once it's SOLD. Actual returns from farming are pitiful compared to the value of the land. If you're going to whack a bill on these grieving families based on what the farm is worth, they CAN'T pay it. They'll have to sell. How on earth do people not understand this? 

The impact of these changes may not be felt by the wider population next Christmas, or the one after that - but once significant numbers of farmers pass away, the British farming community will be changed forever. 

Farming is a very lonely business. Up early, out all day, often with just your own thoughts. All to scrape a living, in the hope that one day you can pass your farm down to your children - just as your parents did for you. That's the whole point. That's why farmers do what they do. 

Labour have snatched that dream away from thousands of farming families. I certainly won't forgive them, and the British farming community won't either.

Take a moment this Christmas to think about where your food comes from, the work that goes into providing it, and who is behind all of that.

British farmers, on British farms.

Tomorrow, Conservatives are forcing a vote on the two-child benefit cap. Why?

Because families on benefits should make the same responsible decisions about having children as everyone else.

The two-child cap is about fairness. Most working families plan their finances carefully. They budget based on what they can afford.

They shouldn’t pay more in tax so others can make different choices without consequences.

Before the cap, families on benefits could receive extra payments for every additional child—regardless of circumstance.

Working households were expected to foot the bill. That wasn’t fair or sustainable.

So in 2017, a Conservative Government introduced the cap.

It restored 3 basic principles:

👉 Support from the state comes with expectations
👉 Work should pay
👉 Welfare must be sustainable
We made progress. But it’s now under threat.

Labour’s Left want to scrap the cap. Reform want the same—unlimited handouts with no plan to pay for them.

And Keir Starmer? Still dodging the question. He won’t say where he stands.

Scrapping the cap would cost £3.5 billion.

That money comes from one place: working families who are already paying record taxes.

They shouldn’t be asked to pay more so others don’t have to make the same life choices.

Tomorrow’s vote is a test: Do you believe in a welfare system that’s fair, affordable, and focused—or not?

Every MP, including Keir Starmer, will have to answer.

Only the Conservatives are standing up for working families.

Born and raised in Carrick Hill, Patrick was a loving son and brother, and a devoted husband and father.

His life was cruelly and brutally taken from him by a serving British soldier from a regiment notorious for its barbarity and discriminate violence.

I will continue to stand with the Quails and all families seeking truth, justice, accountability and respect.

Heavy rainfall and flooding at the start of the year caused chaos in some of our villages, and I have been raising this both locally and down in Parliament. 

One problem has been the dip in the road at Fenn Lanes by the Dadlington Crossroads which has been flooded for quite some time. After the water cleared, the road remained closed - causing significant disruption to local people. 

Many people have raised the impact of the road closures with me and I shared their concerns with Leicestershire County Council, which is responsible for highways and flood prevention and drain maintenance in our area.

Here is their response:

'Apologies for the delay in replying to your emails regarding Fenn Lanes.
 
Regarding the water being removed and the road closure staying in place, this was due to the unsafe conditions of the carriageway following the flooding event.
 
We closed the road when we had the report of the depth of the water and vehicles becoming unable to pass. Unfortunately one vehicle was abandoned within the flood water and many vehicles were ignoring the road closure at the time. This unfortunately led to severe damage to the edge of the carriageway and the exposure of utilities within the verge.
 
As the conditions were not safe Leicestershire County Council took the decision that the road closure would have to remain in place.
 
We have a drainage team attending today [10/02/2025] to work on Fenn Lanes to carry out the necessary repairs to enable the carriageway to be reopened. We will be then working on Shenton Lane which is at the same cross roads. Fortunately at the time of the flooding event the water receded on Shenton Lane and the closure was not required to stay in place.
 
Works are also to be undertaken with a high pressure combi unit to cleanse and check the drainage network in the vicinity following the necessary repair works, but these works will require the road to be closed again for safety.'
